```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
has_modelcompR <- requireNamespace("modelcompR", quietly = TRUE)
has_symcompR <- requireNamespace("symcompR", quietly = TRUE)
has_z3r <- requireNamespace("z3r", quietly = TRUE)
has_optcompR <- requireNamespace("optcompR", quietly = TRUE)
has_jaxR <- requireNamespace("jaxR", quietly = TRUE) &&
  isTRUE(tryCatch(jaxR:::backend_available(), error = function(e) FALSE))
has_luz <- requireNamespace("luz", quietly = TRUE)
has_generics <- requireNamespace("generics", quietly = TRUE)
has_torch <- torch::torch_is_installed()
```

```{r setup}
library(graphlearnR)
```

graphlearnR is one of a series of R packages by the same author. The graph
learning engine depends only on `torch`, `igraph` and `Matrix`; every
connection to a sibling package is optional, lives in `Suggests`, and
fails with a clear message when the sibling is not installed. This article
shows one bridge per package (modelcompR, symcompR, z3r, optcompR, jaxR)
and the connections to luz and tidymodels.

The code chunks below run only when the sibling package is installed. On
the package website they ran if the build machine had it.

## Graph dynamics with modelcompR

[modelcompR](https://github.com/adamrsophie/modelcompR) solves
differential equations. `graph_diffusion()` uses it to simulate heat
diffusion on a graph,
$$\frac{du}{dt} = -\kappa L u,$$
where $L$ is the graph Laplacian. graphlearnR builds the operator and
modelcompR integrates it; graphlearnR has no ODE solver of its own.

```{r, eval = has_modelcompR}
g <- graph_data(edge_index = rbind(c(1, 2, 3, 3), c(2, 3, 4, 5)), num_nodes = 5,
                directed = FALSE)
u <- graph_diffusion(g, u0 = c(1, 0, 0, 0, 0), times = c(0, 0.5, 1, 2, 5, 20))
round(u, 3)
rowSums(u)
```

Heat flows from node 1 to the rest; the total stays at one because the
plain Laplacian conserves it on an undirected graph, and every node tends
to the mean, 0.2. The test suite checks the solution against the
closed form $e^{-\kappa t L} u_0$ computed from an eigendecomposition.

This is a mechanistic simulation tool. modelcompR solves on R numerics,
so gradients do not flow back into torch, and `graph_diffusion()` is not a
neural ODE layer. Diffusion outputs can still be used as fixed node
features, for example heat kernel signatures at a few times:

```{r, eval = has_modelcompR}
heat <- sapply(seq_len(num_nodes(g)), function(i) {
  e <- numeric(num_nodes(g))
  e[i] <- 1
  graph_diffusion(g, e, times = c(0, 1))[2, i]
})
round(heat, 3)
```

Node 3, the hub, keeps the least of its own heat after one time unit.

## Exact operators with symcompR

[symcompR](https://github.com/adamrsophie/symcompR) is a computer algebra
system. `graph_operator_symbolic()` returns the adjacency matrix, the
Laplacian, or the GCN propagation matrix
$\hat D^{-1/2}(A + I)\hat D^{-1/2}$ with exact entries, so the
normalization a layer applies can be read off directly.

```{r, eval = has_symcompR}
path <- graph_data(edge_index = rbind(1:3, 2:4), num_nodes = 4, directed = FALSE)
P <- graph_operator_symbolic(path, "gcn")
P
```

The square roots stay exact. `as.matrix()` gives the numeric values, which
match what `gcn_conv()` computes when its weight is the identity:

```{r, eval = has_symcompR && has_torch}
layer <- gcn_conv(4, 4, bias = FALSE)
invisible(torch::with_no_grad(layer$lin$weight$copy_(torch::torch_eye(4))))
out <- as.matrix(layer(torch::torch_eye(4), graph_tensors(path)$edge_index))
all.equal(out, as.matrix(P), tolerance = 1e-6, check.attributes = FALSE)
```

The bridge targets small graphs: exact arithmetic is slow and each entry
is a symbolic object.

## Rule constrained labels with z3r

[z3r](https://github.com/adamrsophie/z3r) gives access to the Z3 solver.
`consistent_labels()` takes per node class probabilities and logical rules
on edges, such as "two adjacent nodes cannot both be in class a", and
finds the most probable labeling that obeys every rule with Z3's
optimizer. Nodes with known labels can be fixed.

```{r, eval = has_z3r}
p <- rbind(c(a = 0.9, b = 0.1), c(a = 0.6, b = 0.4), c(a = 0.7, b = 0.3), c(a = 0.2, b = 0.8))
ring <- rbind(c(1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 4, 4, 1), c(2, 1, 3, 2, 4, 3, 1, 4))
res <- consistent_labels(p, ring, forbidden = cbind("a", "a"))
res$labels
res$changed
```

Independent predictions would label nodes 1, 2 and 3 as a; the rule allows
no two neighbors in a, and the cheapest fix in log probability changes
node 2. This runs after training on small graphs; it is a combinatorial
search, not a differentiable layer. The continuous integration runners
ship a Z3 release older than z3r needs, so this bridge is tested on
machines with a newer Z3 only.

## Budgeted link selection with optcompR

[optcompR](https://github.com/adamrsophie/optcompR) builds and solves
optimization models. `select_links()` chooses which predicted links to add
under a budget and a cap on new links per node, maximizing the total
score: a 0-1 integer program solved with HiGHS.

```{r, eval = has_optcompR && has_torch}
sbm <- dataset_sbm(c(30, 30), seed = 1)
split <- split_edges(sbm, seed = 1)
torch::torch_manual_seed(1)
fit_link <- train_graph_model(gnn_model("gcn", ncol(sbm$x), 16), split, "link_prediction",
                              epochs = 50, seed = 1)
cand <- split$test_pos
prob <- predict(fit_link, pairs = cand, type = "prob")
pick <- select_links(cand, prob, budget = 5, max_new_degree = 1)
pick$pairs
round(prob[pick$selected], 3)
```

Integer programs are not differentiable, so this is a decision step after
training, as the design brief requires.

## A second array backend with jaxR

[jaxR](https://github.com/adamrsophie/jaxR) brings JAX's transformations
to R. `aggregate_jax()` is the neighborhood aggregation of
`message_passing()` written in jaxR array operations, so it composes with
`jaxR::grad()`, `jaxR::vmap()` and `jaxR::jit()`. The tests check its
values and gradients against the torch version.

```{r, eval = has_jaxR}
g_small <- graph_data(x = matrix(1:8, 4, 2), edge_index = rbind(c(1, 2, 3, 4), c(2, 3, 4, 2)),
                      num_nodes = 4)
as.matrix(aggregate_jax(g_small$x, g_small$edge_index, aggr = "mean"))
f <- function(x) jaxR::jnp_sum(aggregate_jax(x, g_small$edge_index, num_nodes = 4L)^2)
as.matrix(jaxR::grad(f)(jaxR::as_jax(g_small$x)))
```

Layers and training stay on torch; models are not converted between
backends. jaxR needs its XLA runtime (`jaxR::install_pjrt()`).

## Training with luz

[luz](https://mlverse.github.io/luz/) is the high level training library
of the torch ecosystem. `luz_node_dataloader()` and `luz_node_module`
adapt a node classification problem to it: the dataloader yields the full
graph with the indices of the masked nodes, and the module returns
predictions for those nodes only.

```{r, eval = has_luz && has_torch}
library(luz)
gk <- split_nodes(dataset_karate(), seed = 1)
torch::torch_manual_seed(1)
fitted <- luz_node_module |>
  setup(loss = torch::nn_cross_entropy_loss(), optimizer = torch::optim_adam,
        metrics = list(luz_metric_accuracy())) |>
  set_hparams(model = gnn_model("gcn", 34, 16, 2)) |>
  set_opt_hparams(lr = 0.01) |>
  fit(luz_node_dataloader(gk, "train"), epochs = 50, verbose = FALSE,
      valid_data = luz_node_dataloader(gk, "val"),
      accelerator = accelerator(cpu = TRUE))
unlist(tail(fitted$records$metrics$valid, 1))
```

`train_graph_model()` remains the main trainer: it also covers sampled
batches, link, edge and graph tasks, and records a reproducibility trail.

## Tidy summaries

`augment()` and `glance()` from the generics package, the verbs used
across tidymodels, work on a `graph_fit`. `augment()` adds the true outcome
and the split of each node to the predictions, ready for yardstick.

```{r, eval = has_generics && has_torch}
fit_k <- train_graph_model(gnn_model("gcn", 34, 8, 2), gk, "node_classification",
                           epochs = 30, seed = 1)
aug <- generics::augment(fit_k)
head(aug)
with(aug[aug$.split == "test", ], mean(.pred_class == .truth))
generics::glance(fit_k)
```

Graph models need the whole graph at prediction time, so there is no
parsnip engine.
